fields: For each instrument, every place it reads (an island or block for the Law Sphere and the counts; a region for the globe) is tested: the sample's count at the place against the count the healthy atlas expects there at the sample's own read depth and cell mix, judged against the spread measured among healthy libraries (not counting alone), with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery control across that instrument's places. Each place named is given its chromosome and position, its CpG island context (island, shore, shelf, open sea), its genes (promoter: within 2 kb of a transcription start; gene body; or the nearest gene and its distance), and whether any array probe covers it. Since a chain update every place is read: all 592,067 Law Sphere units over the 28,217,448 hg19 CpGs (islands, and 50-CpG blocks between them), against a healthy reference and measured null built from all 156 Sequencing Atlas inputs over every unit. Since a chain update each named place is read again CpG by CpG from the sample's own molecules: a place whose excess sits at one or two CpGs, changed on most of the molecules covering them, is printed as 'probable genetic variant at a CpG' with the CpG and not counted as a change of methylation (a variant such as C to T changes one CpG on every molecule that carries it; a change of methylation spreads over the place).
A score says how much a sample changed; a researcher also needs to know where, and which genes, to compare with expression, with other studies and across patients.

592,067 places (CpG islands, then 50-CpG blocks) and 28,218 regions; places by RefSeq relation: promoter 104,607, gene body 254,895, intergenic 232,565; by context: island 95,089, shore 35,892, shelf 21,335, open sea 439,751; 18,755 promoter places without an array probe. Planted tests on GSM5652214: 9 of 10 gain islands found, loss blocks named at 6.3 times their healthy level and above, none below 3.3; no place named in any healthy or unplanted read (every loss and gain unit tested).

Positions reference built from public UCSC hg19 files and checked against all 813,951 array probe positions; healthy null by leave-one-out over the 205 atlas libraries; planted-place tests for detection.

Known-answer library GSM5652214 through the one button: unplanted, 0 places except one island marked as a probable genetic variant (147 of 152 held molecules changed at one CpG in ABCA2; the guard counts 0 changes); planted, gain side 18-19 of 20 planted islands with no other place; loss side by added lost marks per 50-CpG block: under 10, 0 of 4; 10-19, 11 of 83; 20-39, 20 of 30; 40 or more, 3 of 3; no false place in any of six reads; no planted place marked as a variant.

Detection depends on depth: at about 30-fold, a loss block expecting about 5 held errors is named once it shows about 4 to 6 times that (finding ); each report prints its own sample's limit, so 'nothing found' is read against it. Promoter calls depend on the gene table (both kept). Positions are hg19. On every place the false-discovery cut is about 20 times stricter than on the type-informative units alone, so a single 50-CpG loss block at this depth is named reliably only from about 20-40 added lost marks; loss spread thinly over many blocks is read by the grouped regions. The variant guard reads named places only.

records.name: The Locator: naming the places that changed, and the genes there
questions: How do you know a named place is not just noise?

Each place is judged against how far healthy libraries actually stray there (measured on the 205 atlas libraries), not against counting alone, with false-discovery control. In every healthy and unplanted read so far, no place was named; planted places were found (9 of 10 planted gains; loss blocks at 6.3 times their healthy level and above).
Why do the gene calls follow one study's definitions?

So named genes compare directly with that study's published gene lists: promoter within 2 kb of a transcription start, shores within 2 kb of an island, shelves 2 to 4 kb. Both RefSeq and the UCSC known-genes table are given, since the second calls more promoters.
What does 'array-blind' mean for a gene?
No array probe covers that place, so no array study could have measured it. 18,755 of the Locator's promoter places (RefSeq) have no probe.
